passages.title: Moses recalls the failed entry
passages.summary: Moses speaks to all Israel east of the Jordan in the fortieth year. He recalls how the LORD told them at Horeb to go and take the land. He recalls choosing leaders and judges to share his load. At Kadesh the people asked for spies, who brought back good fruit. Still the people refused to go up and said the LORD hated them. The LORD swore that generation would not see the land, except Caleb and Joshua. Moses says the LORD was angry with him too. The people then went up without the LORD and were beaten back.

lds.text: Moses tells the children what their parents did at Kadesh. What does he say about himself in verse 37?

contextNote.title: A speech to the next generation retains the cost of earlier choices
contextNote.text: Moses is speaking to the children of the people who refused at Kadesh. He says “you” throughout, as if they had been there (verses 26–27). The parents’ choice is told as the family’s own history. In verse 37 he adds his own loss: he also will not enter. He says it was “for your sakes,” tying his fate to theirs. Numbers 20:12 gives the reason as Moses’s own act at the rock. So the speech keeps the cost of the past in front of a new generation.

passages.title: Neighboring lands and Sihon
passages.summary: Israel wandered around Mount Seir for many days. The LORD told them not to fight Esau’s people and to pay for food. He gave Moab and Ammon to Lot’s children, so Israel must leave them alone. Other peoples had also replaced earlier peoples in those lands. Thirty-eight years passed until the fighting men of the first generation died. Then the LORD gave Sihon the Amorite into Israel’s hand. Moses sent Sihon words of peace, and Sihon refused. Israel defeated him and destroyed his cities.

lds.text: Why must Israel leave some neighboring lands alone? What reason does verse 5 give about Mount Seir?

contextNote.title: The land promise does not give Israel every neighboring territory
contextNote.text: Israel is on its way to land God promised. Verse 5 says the promise has edges. Mount Seir belongs to Esau, “because I have given” it to him. Verses 9 and 19 say the same of Moab and Ammon, Lot’s children. So the LORD gives land to other peoples too, and Israel must respect it. Israel is to buy food and water there, not take it (verse 6). Sihon’s land is given to Israel, and he refuses peace (verses 24–30).

passages.title: Og, eastern settlements, and Joshua
passages.summary: Og king of Bashan comes out to fight, and the LORD gives him to Israel. Israel takes his sixty walled cities. Moses gives the land east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. Their fighting men must still cross and help their brothers. Moses tells Joshua not to fear the kingdoms ahead. Moses begs the LORD to let him cross and see the good land. The LORD refuses and tells him to look from the top of Pisgah. He must strengthen Joshua, who will lead the people over.

lds.text: Moses asks to cross the Jordan, and the LORD says no (verses 25–27). What task is he given in verse 28?

contextNote.title: Moses must prepare a successor for work he cannot finish
contextNote.text: Moses’s prayer in verses 24–25 is personal: let me see the good land. The answer is a flat no: “Speak no more to me of this matter.” He may look from a mountain but not cross (verse 27). Verse 28 turns at once to what he can still do. He is to appoint Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him. Joshua will finish the work, and Moses must make him ready for it. Verses 21–22 show Moses already doing this.

passages.title: Remember the covenant
passages.summary: Moses tells Israel to keep the statutes and not add or take away. Other nations will call Israel wise for having such laws and so near a God. They must not forget Horeb, where the mountain burned and they heard a voice. They saw no form, so they must make no image of any creature. They must not worship the sun, moon, or stars. If they make idols, they will be scattered among the nations. Yet if they seek the LORD there with all their heart, they will find him. Moses sets apart three cities of refuge east of the Jordan.

lds.text: What helps you teach God’s commands with care? At Horeb Israel “saw no kind of form” (verse 15). What did they have in its place (verse 12)?

contextNote.title: A remembered voice limits what an image can claim
contextNote.text: Verse 12 states what happened at Horeb: a voice, and no form. Verse 15 draws the rule from that fact. Because they saw no shape, they may make no shape to stand for God. Verses 16–18 close every door: human, animal, bird, creeping thing, fish. What Israel was given is words, written on two tablets (verse 13). So God is remembered by his words, taught to children (verse 9). An image would claim to show what no one saw.

passages.title: The commandments recalled
passages.summary: Moses calls all Israel to hear the statutes. He says the covenant at Horeb was made with those alive today. He repeats the ten commandments. The Sabbath command says servants must rest as well as their masters. Israel must remember it was a servant in Egypt until the LORD brought it out. The LORD wrote the words on two stone tablets. The people were afraid of the fire and asked Moses to listen for them. The LORD approved and wished they would always have such a heart.

lds.text: Verse 15 gives a reason for the Sabbath. What must Israel remember?

contextNote.title: The command to rest receives an explanation rooted in slavery
contextNote.text: Exodus 20:11 tied the Sabbath to God’s rest at creation. Verse 15 gives a second reason: “you were a servant in the land of Egypt.” Verse 14 says servants must rest “as well as you.” A master must remember being a slave when he sees his workers. Pharaoh gave Israel no rest (Exodus 5:5–9). So the weekly rest is a way of not becoming Pharaoh. Verse 3 adds that the covenant is with the living hearers, not only their parents.

passages.title: Love, teach, and remember
passages.summary: Moses gives the commandments Israel must keep in the land. The LORD is one, and Israel must love him with heart, soul, and might. These words must be on their hearts and taught to their children. They talk of them at home, on the road, at night, and at dawn. They are to tie them on hand and forehead and write them on doorposts. In the land they will have cities, houses, wells, and vineyards they did not make. Then they must not forget the LORD. When a son asks what the laws mean, the parent tells of slavery and rescue.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies love for God and teaching the next generation. Verse 7 names four times to talk of God’s words. What are they?

contextNote.title: Memory needs daily practice
contextNote.text: Verse 5 asks for love with the whole person. Verse 6 says where the words must be: on the heart. Verse 7 turns that inward state into a daily habit with children. The four settings cover a whole day: sitting, walking, lying down, rising. No special place or teacher is named. Verses 10–12 show why the habit is needed: full houses make people forget. Verse 20 expects it to work, since the child starts asking questions.

passages.title: A chosen people and severe commands
passages.summary: Moses says the LORD will drive out seven nations greater than Israel. Israel is told to destroy them, make no treaty, and not marry among them. The reason given is that they would turn Israel to other gods. Israel must break their altars and burn their images. The LORD chose Israel, though it was the fewest of all peoples. He chose it because he loves it and keeps his oath to the fathers. If Israel obeys, he will bless its children, crops, and herds. The nations will be driven out little by little.

lds.text: Read covenant responsibilities beside the harm described in the chapter. Keep ancient commands distinct from present Church conduct. Verse 7 says why God did not choose Israel. What reason does verse 8 give for his choice?

contextNote.title: Chosen status does not rest on numerical strength
contextNote.text: Verses 1–5 give Israel hard orders against seven nations. Verse 6 calls Israel chosen, and verse 7 blocks a proud reading of that word. They were not more in number; they were the fewest. Verse 8 gives two reasons, and both lie in God: his love and his oath. So being chosen is not a reward for strength or goodness. Verse 4 gives the stated reason for the harsh orders: the pull of other gods. The chapter states those orders plainly and does not soften them.

passages.title: Remember in prosperity
passages.summary: Moses tells Israel to remember the forty years in the wilderness. God humbled them, let them hunger, and fed them with manna. He taught them that people do not live by bread alone. Their clothes did not wear out, and their feet did not swell. Now he brings them to a land of water, wheat, vines, olives, and metal. When they are full and rich, they must not forget the LORD. They must not say their own power got this wealth. If they forget and serve other gods, they will perish like the nations before them.

lds.text: The Church lesson asks readers to remember God in comfort as well as hardship. What might a full person say “in your heart” (verse 17)? How does verse 18 answer?

contextNote.title: Success can hide the conditions that made it possible
contextNote.text: The danger in this chapter is plenty, not hunger. Verses 12–13 list good houses, growing herds, silver, and gold. Verse 14 says a full heart is “lifted up” and forgets. Verse 17 gives the thought that follows: my own hand got me this wealth. In the wilderness no one could think that, since manna fell each day. Verse 18 corrects it: God gives the power to get wealth. He gives it to keep the covenant he swore, not to prove their worth.

passages.title: The calf and intercession recalled
passages.summary: Israel is about to cross the Jordan against nations greater and taller. The LORD will go ahead like a devouring fire. Israel must not say the land is a reward for its righteousness. The nations are driven out for their wickedness and because of God’s oath. Israel is a stubborn people, and Moses tells them to remember it. He recalls the golden calf, the broken tablets, and forty days of prayer. He names Taberah, Massah, Kibroth Hattaavah, and Kadesh. He prayed that God would remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and spare his people.

lds.text: Moses says three times the land is no reward for goodness (verses 4–6). What does he call Israel in verse 6?

contextNote.title: Possessing the land does not prove the people's innocence
contextNote.text: Winning a land could make a people think they deserved it. Verses 4, 5, and 6 each deny that. The nations lose the land for their wickedness. Israel gains it because of God’s oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Verse 6 adds a hard name for Israel: “a stiff-necked people.” Verses 7–24 back it up with the calf and four other failures. So possession of the land proves God’s faithfulness, not Israel’s merit.

passages.title: New tablets and care for strangers
passages.summary: Moses recalls cutting two new tablets and making a wooden ark for them. The LORD wrote the ten commandments again, and Moses put them in the ark. Aaron died, and the tribe of Levi was set apart to carry the ark. The LORD listened to Moses and did not destroy Israel. Now the LORD asks Israel to fear him, love him, and keep his commands. He owns heaven and earth, yet he set his love on their fathers. He takes no bribes and gives justice to the fatherless and widow. He loves the foreigner, so Israel must love the foreigner too.

lds.text: Verse 19 tells Israel to love the foreigner. What two reasons do verses 18–19 give?

contextNote.title: Remembered exclusion becomes a duty toward resident outsiders
contextNote.text: Verse 17 describes God at his greatest: God of gods, mighty, taking no bribes. Verse 18 says what that great God does. He gives justice to the fatherless and widow and feeds and clothes the foreigner. Verse 19 draws the command from his example: “Therefore love the foreigner.” It adds Israel’s own memory: “you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” So the duty has two roots, who God is and what Israel went through. Verse 16 calls this a change of heart, not only of rules.

passages.title: Teach the words and choose a path
passages.summary: Moses tells those who saw Egypt and the wilderness to love the LORD. The land ahead is not like Egypt, where they watered fields by foot. It is a land of hills and valleys that drinks rain from the sky. The LORD’s eyes are on it all year. If Israel obeys, he will send early and late rain. If they turn to other gods, he will shut the sky. They must teach these words to their children and write them on their doorposts. Moses sets a blessing and a curse before them, on Gerizim and Ebal.

lds.text: Egypt’s fields were watered by foot, and Canaan’s by rain (verses 10–11). On whom does a rain-fed land depend?

contextNote.title: A description of farming turns the land into a place of dependence
contextNote.text: Verse 10 recalls Egyptian farming: water moved to the seed “with your foot.” The farmer there brought the water himself. Verse 11 says Canaan “drinks water from the rain of the sky.” No one can make it rain. So the new land ties each harvest to the one who sends rain (verse 14). Verses 16–17 state the risk: other gods, a shut sky, no fruit. The land itself becomes a daily lesson in dependence.

passages.title: The chosen place of worship
passages.summary: Israel must destroy the places where the nations served their gods. They must not worship the LORD that way, at every hill and tree. They are to bring offerings and tithes to the one place he will choose. There they eat and rejoice with sons, daughters, servants, and the Levite. They may kill and eat meat in any town, as they would a deer. But they must pour out the blood and not eat it. Holy gifts and vows still go to the chosen place. They must not copy the nations, who even burn their children for their gods.

lds.text: Keep the text’s unnamed sanctuary distinct from a later identification. Offerings go to one chosen place (verse 14). What does verse 15 allow in every town?

contextNote.title: A central place of worship does not control every meal
contextNote.text: Verses 5–14 gather all offerings into one place that God will choose. That could seem to make every meal of meat a long journey. Verse 15 prevents this. People may kill and eat “within all your gates,” like game. The unclean and the clean may both eat it, so it is ordinary food. Only the blood rule follows them home (verse 16). The text never names the chosen place.

passages.title: Tests of covenant loyalty
passages.summary: A prophet may give a sign that comes true and then urge other gods. Israel must not listen, because the LORD is testing their love. That prophet is to be put to death. If a brother, child, wife, or close friend secretly urges other gods, the same applies. The one who was urged must not hide it. If a town is said to have turned, the report must be checked with care. If it is true, the town is destroyed and burned. Nothing from it may be kept.

lds.text: Keep this ancient punishment system distinct from present conduct. A sign may come true and still mislead (verses 1–3). What does verse 3 say the LORD is testing?

contextNote.title: A striking sign does not settle whether a message should be followed
contextNote.text: Verse 2 grants that the sign “comes to pass.” The test is not whether the wonder is real. The test is where the message leads: “Let’s go after other gods.” A true sign joined to that call must be refused (verse 3). So a message is judged by loyalty to the LORD who freed them (verse 5). Verse 14 adds a rule for rumor: inquire, investigate, and ask diligently. The penalties are severe, and the town’s case requires proof first.

passages.title: Food, tithes, and shared provision
passages.summary: Israel is the LORD’s children and must not cut themselves for the dead. They may eat cud-chewing animals with split hooves, and fish with fins and scales. Camels, hares, pigs, and many birds are forbidden. Each year they eat a tenth of their crops at the chosen place. If the way is far, they may bring money and buy food there. They must not forget the Levite. Every third year the tithe is stored in their own towns. The Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow come and eat their fill.

lds.text: Every third year the tithe stays in the town (verse 28). Who eats from it in verse 29?

contextNote.title: A tithe can serve people who lack a secure household share
contextNote.text: In most years the family eats its tithe at the chosen place (verses 22–26). Verse 28 changes the plan every third year. The whole tithe is stored “within your gates,” in the home town. Verse 29 names four groups: the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. The Levite has no land, and the others have no secure provider. They are to “eat and be satisfied,” not just get by. The blessing on the farmer’s work is tied to this sharing.

passages.title: Release and an open hand
passages.summary: Every seven years a creditor must cancel what a fellow Israelite owes. If Israel obeys, there will be no poor among them. They must open their hand to a poor brother and lend what he needs. They must not refuse a loan because the year of release is near. They must give freely, because there will always be poor in the land. A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year. He must be sent away with gifts from flock, grain, and wine. Firstborn male animals belong to the LORD.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies a willing heart in helping people in need. What “wicked thought” does verse 9 warn a lender against?

contextNote.title: An approaching release must not become an excuse to refuse help
contextNote.text: Verse 1 cancels debts every seventh year. That creates a temptation, and verse 9 names it. A lender could refuse a loan that will soon be wiped out. The verse calls that thought wicked, and the poor may cry to the LORD. Verse 10 asks for more than the loan: a heart that does not grudge it. Verses 13–14 say a freed servant must not leave empty-handed. Verse 15 gives the reason: Israel was a slave, and the LORD redeemed it.

passages.title: Festivals and fair judgment
passages.summary: Israel keeps the Passover in the month of Abib, at the place the LORD chooses. They eat unleavened bread seven days, the bread of affliction. Seven weeks after harvest begins, they keep the feast of weeks with a free gift. They rejoice with children, servants, Levites, foreigners, the fatherless, and widows. They keep the feast of booths seven days after the harvest is in. Three times a year the men come before the LORD with a gift. Judges in every town must judge fairly and take no bribe. No sacred pole or pillar may stand by the LORD’s altar.

lds.text: Verse 11 lists who must share the feast’s joy. Who is on the list besides the family?

contextNote.title: Festival joy reaches beyond the people who own its resources
contextNote.text: The feast of weeks comes at harvest, when a landowner has the most. Verse 11 says who must rejoice with him. The list starts with his children and servants. It goes on to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. Verse 14 repeats the same list for the feast of booths. Verse 12 gives the reason: “you were a slave in Egypt.” A feast kept only by the harvest’s owners is not the feast commanded here.

passages.title: Judges and limits on kings
passages.summary: No animal with a defect may be offered to the LORD. Serving other gods brings death, but only on two or three witnesses. Hard cases go to the priests and the judge at the chosen place. Their verdict must be followed. Israel may one day ask for a king like other nations. He must be an Israelite whom the LORD chooses. He must not collect many horses, wives, or much silver and gold. He must write his own copy of this law and read it all his life.

lds.text: Which rules stop a king from using his power only for himself (verses 16–17)? What must he read every day (verses 18–19)?

contextNote.title: The king must live under the law
contextNote.text: Verses 16–17 limit three things a king might gather: horses, wives, and treasure. Verse 16 ties horses to going back to Egypt, which is forbidden. Verses 18–19 give him a task: copy the law and read it daily. Verse 20 states the aim: “that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers.” The king is called a brother and stays under the same law as everyone. First Kings 10:26–11:4 reports that Solomon broke all three limits.

passages.title: Priests and a prophet like Moses
passages.summary: The priests and Levites have no land, and the LORD is their inheritance. They receive set parts of sacrifices and the first of grain, wine, oil, and wool. A Levite from any town may come and serve at the chosen place. Israel must not copy the nations who burn children, tell fortunes, or consult the dead. The LORD will raise up a prophet like Moses from among them. Israel asked for this at Horeb, when they feared God’s voice. A prophet who speaks falsely in God’s name must die. If what a prophet says does not happen, the LORD did not say it.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the prophet like Moses with Christ. Verse 21 asks how to know a word the LORD did not speak. What test does verse 22 give?

contextNote.title: A prophet's claim requires attention to what actually happens
contextNote.text: Verses 10–14 forbid the usual ways of learning the future: fortunes, omens, the dead. Verse 15 gives Israel a prophet in their place. That raises a problem, and verse 21 asks it openly. How can people tell a true word from a false one? Verse 22 gives a test anyone can apply: watch whether it happens. A failed word frees the people from fear of that speaker. Chapter 13 added a second test: a sign that comes true may still lead astray.

passages.title: Refuge, boundaries, and witnesses
passages.summary: Israel must set apart three cities in the land for anyone who kills by accident. An example is an ax head that flies off and strikes a neighbor. The cities keep the avenger from killing him in hot anger. If the land grows, three more cities are added. A man who kills from hatred is handed over to die. No one may move a neighbor’s boundary stone. A charge needs two or three witnesses, not one. A false witness receives the penalty he meant for the other person.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: One witness is not enough for any charge (verse 15). What happens to a witness who lies (verses 18–19)?

contextNote.title: A serious accusation requires more than one person's assertion
contextNote.text: A single accuser can be mistaken or can lie. Verse 15 says no charge of any kind stands on one voice. Two or three must agree. Verses 16–18 deal with a witness who lies on purpose. The judges must “make diligent inquisition” and not simply take his word. If he lied, he gets the penalty he sought for his brother (verse 19). So the court protects the accused as well as the victim.

passages.title: Rules for warfare
passages.summary: Before battle a priest tells the army the LORD fights for them. Officers send home men with a new house, vineyard, or bride. They also send home anyone who is afraid. A distant city must first be offered peace. If it refuses, its men are killed and the rest are taken. Cities of the land itself must be destroyed, to keep Israel from their gods. During a long siege Israel must not cut down fruit trees. Only trees that give no food may be used for siege works.

lds.text: Read the restraints and the violence together. Keep ancient war law distinct from present religious duty. What reason does verse 19 give for sparing fruit trees?

contextNote.title: The rules restrain some destruction while requiring other destruction
contextNote.text: This chapter holds limits and harsh orders side by side. Verses 5–8 send men home for a house, a vineyard, a marriage, or fear. Verse 10 requires an offer of peace before a siege. Verses 16–17 order the complete destruction of the cities of the land. Verse 19 then protects fruit trees with a question: is the tree a man? An army will need that food later, and the tree has not fought anyone. The text restrains waste while it commands killing, and it does not reconcile the two.

passages.title: Unsolved killing and household laws
passages.summary: When a slain body is found and no killer is known, the nearest elders act. They break a heifer’s neck, wash their hands, and ask the LORD’s forgiveness. A soldier who marries a captive woman must first give her a month to mourn. If he later sends her away, he may not sell her. A man with two wives must give the firstborn’s double share to the true firstborn. He may not favor the son of the wife he loves. Parents may bring a stubborn, rebellious son to the elders, and he is stoned. A hanged body must be buried the same day.

lds.text: Consider whose voice is absent from these laws. Keep the ancient penalties distinct from present family conduct. Why can a father not pass over his firstborn in verses 15–17?

contextNote.title: A father's preference cannot remove every inheritance claim
contextNote.text: Verse 15 pictures a man with two wives, one loved and one “hated.” Jacob’s house was like that, with Leah and Rachel (Genesis 29:30–31). The father might want to honor the loved wife’s son. Verse 16 says he may not. Verse 17 gives the double share to the actual firstborn, whoever his mother is. So a son’s right does not depend on his father’s feelings toward his mother. The law limits a father’s power inside his own house.

passages.title: Neighborly care and sexual laws
passages.summary: Anyone who finds a neighbor’s stray animal or lost item must return it. A fallen animal must be helped up. A mother bird must be let go when the young are taken. A new house needs a railing around its roof so no one falls. Seeds, plow animals, and cloth types must not be mixed. A husband who falsely accuses his bride is fined, and a guilty bride is stoned. Adultery brings death for both. A woman forced in the open country is not guilty, and only the man dies.

lds.text: What duties here protect others from harm? The sexual laws reflect ancient rules about marriage and family honor. What must a builder add to a new roof (verse 8)?

contextNote.title: A home's design can create responsibility before anyone falls
contextNote.text: Verse 8 assumes people will be up on the roof. It puts a duty on the builder before any accident happens. He must add a railing. If he does not and someone falls, the blood is “on your house.” So a person answers for a danger he could foresee and did not fix. Verses 1–4 say the same about a neighbor’s animals: “You may not hide yourself.” Doing nothing is treated as a choice.

passages.title: Assembly, camp, and promises
passages.summary: Some people may not enter the LORD’s assembly. Ammonites and Moabites are barred, because they refused bread and hired Balaam. Edomites and Egyptians are not to be hated, and their third generation may enter. The army camp must be kept clean, because the LORD walks in it. An escaped servant must not be handed back to his master. He may live where he chooses and must not be oppressed. Israel must not charge a brother interest and must pay its vows. A person may eat in a neighbor’s field but not carry food away.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Keep ancient membership restrictions distinct from present human worth. An escaped servant is not sent back (verse 15). Where may he live, according to verse 16?

contextNote.title: An escaped servant receives protection from forced return
contextNote.text: A runaway servant has no power, and his master has a claim on him. Verse 15 still forbids Israel to hand him over. Verse 16 goes further and gives him the choice of where to live. He may settle “where it pleases him best,” and no one may oppress him. Israel had itself fled from a master (Exodus 14:5). Verse 7 uses the same memory to forbid hating Egyptians. The rule places the escaped person’s safety above the owner’s claim.

passages.title: Household changes and protection of the poor
passages.summary: A man who divorces his wife gives her a written certificate. If she remarries and is free again, the first husband may not take her back. A newly married man stays home from war for a year. No one may take a millstone as a pledge, because it is a person’s living. A lender waits outside for a pledge and returns a poor man’s cloak by sunset. A hired worker must be paid the same day. Each person dies for his own sin, not a parent’s or child’s. Forgotten sheaves, olives, and grapes are left for foreigners, the fatherless, and widows.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: A poor worker must be paid before sunset (verse 15). What reason does the verse give?

contextNote.title: Daily wages answer a need that cannot wait indefinitely
contextNote.text: A day worker lives on that day’s pay. Verse 15 says he “is poor and sets his heart on it.” Holding the wage overnight keeps back what he needs now. The verse covers foreigners as well as Israelites (verse 14). It warns that the worker may cry to the LORD against the employer. Verses 6 and 10–13 protect the same people from lenders. Verse 18 gives the ground for all of it: “you were a slave in Egypt.”

passages.title: Fair measures and family continuity
passages.summary: Judges must clear the innocent and condemn the guilty. A beating may not go past forty strokes, so the person is not degraded. An ox must not be muzzled while it treads grain. If a man dies without a son, his brother should marry the widow. If the brother refuses, she removes his sandal before the elders. Israel must not keep two sets of weights or measures. Weights and measures must be full and fair. Israel must remember how Amalek attacked the weak at the rear.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Verse 13 forbids a heavy weight and a light one in the same bag. Why does a fair measure matter when a buyer cannot check it?

contextNote.title: Small measures can cause real harm
contextNote.text: Goods were weighed against weights kept in a bag. Verse 13 pictures a cheat with two sets, one heavy and one light. The buyer has no way to test them. Verse 15 requires one “perfect and just” weight and measure. The reward promised is long life in the land, as for honoring parents (5:16). Verse 16 calls dishonest dealing an abomination to the LORD. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the rule has in view.

passages.title: First produce and covenant declaration
passages.summary: In the land, each Israelite brings a basket of first fruits to the priest. He says that he has come to the land the LORD swore to give. He says his father was a Syrian near death who went to Egypt. Egypt made them slaves, and the LORD heard their cry and brought them out. Now he brings the first of what the LORD gave. He rejoices with the Levite and the foreigner. In the third year he gives the tithe to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow. Israel declares the LORD is its God, and the LORD declares Israel his own people.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: The farmer brings a basket and tells a story (verses 5–10). Where does the story begin?

contextNote.title: Offering crops joins present abundance with a remembered vulnerable past
contextNote.text: The giver stands at the altar with good fruit from his own land. His words in verse 5 start somewhere else: “a Syrian ready to perish.” He names an ancestor with no land and few people. Verses 6–8 go through slavery, a cry, and rescue. Only in verse 10 does he reach the basket. So the gift is set inside a history of weakness and help. Verse 11 then shares the joy with the Levite and the foreigner.

passages.title: Instructions for Ebal and Gerizim
passages.summary: After crossing the Jordan, the people must set up large plastered stones. They must write the law on them plainly, on Mount Ebal. They build an altar there of uncut stones. Six tribes stand on Gerizim to bless and six on Ebal for the curse. The Levites call out twelve curses in a loud voice. The curses name secret idols, dishonoring parents, and moving a boundary stone. They name misleading the blind, denying justice to the weak, and secret killing. After each one, all the people answer, “Amen.”

lds.text: The people answer “Amen” to each curse. What kind of wrong does verse 18 name?

contextNote.title: Public responses name wrongs that can remain hidden
contextNote.text: Many of these twelve curses name acts done out of sight. Verse 15 says an idol set up “in secret,” and verse 24 a secret killing. A moved boundary stone or a bribe may never reach a court. Verse 18 names the blind traveler, who cannot see who misled him. So the list covers wrongs that witnesses and judges would miss. Each person says “Amen” aloud and binds himself. The public oath reaches where public law cannot.

passages.title: Blessings and terrible curses
passages.summary: If Israel listens to the LORD, blessings will overtake them. They will be blessed in city and field, in children, crops, and herds. The LORD will send rain, and they will lend and not borrow. If they do not listen, curses will overtake them. They will suffer sickness, drought, defeat, and loss of all they work for. A far nation whose language they do not know will besiege their towns. They will be scattered among the nations and find no rest. They will even be offered as slaves in Egypt, and no one will buy them.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Read the whole warning with care. Avoid using its suffering language to assign blame to someone in distress. What does verse 47 say Israel failed to do in a time of plenty?

contextNote.title: The warnings describe the loss of an entire way of life
contextNote.text: The blessings fill fourteen verses, and the curses fill fifty-four. Verse 47 gives the root of the curses in one line. Israel did not serve the LORD “with joyfulness” when it had “abundance of all things.” Verse 48 turns each good into its loss: hunger, thirst, nakedness, and lack. The chapter ends in Egypt, where the story of rescue began (verse 68). It warns a nation before it enters the land. It is not a rule for judging one sufferer.

passages.title: The covenant assembly
passages.summary: Moses gathers all Israel in Moab for a covenant beyond the one at Horeb. He recalls Egypt and forty years when their clothes did not wear out. Everyone stands before the LORD: leaders, men, children, wives, and foreigners. Even the woodcutter and the water carrier are there. The covenant is also made with those not present that day. No one who turns to other gods in secret will be pardoned. Later nations will ask why the land was ruined and hear the reason. Secret things belong to the LORD, and revealed things to Israel and its children.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies inward loyalty and shared covenant identity. Who stands in the covenant assembly in verses 10–11?

contextNote.title: The assembly includes people beyond its leaders and warriors
contextNote.text: Verse 10 begins the list with heads, elders, and officers. Verse 11 goes on to little ones, wives, and foreigners in the camp. It ends with the lowest jobs: cutting wood and drawing water. All of them “stand today” before the LORD and enter the covenant. Verses 14–15 stretch it further, to people not yet born. So the covenant is not held only by leaders or fighting men. Verse 29 gives everyone the same task: do the words that have been revealed.

passages.title: Return and choose life
passages.summary: When scattered Israel returns to the LORD, he will gather them. He will bring them back from the farthest places. He will change their hearts so they love him and live. The command is not too hard or too far away. It is not in heaven or across the sea. The word is very near, in their mouth and heart. Moses sets life and death, blessing and curse, before them. He tells them to choose life by loving the LORD and holding to him.

lds.text: The Church lesson compares these words with Lehi’s teaching about agency. The word is “very near to you” (verse 14). What choice does verse 19 set before Israel?

contextNote.title: Near words still require a choice of action
contextNote.text: Verses 12–13 answer two excuses before anyone makes them. The command is not up in heaven, and it is not across the sea. No one has to fetch it. Verse 14 says where it already is: “in your mouth and in your heart.” Moses has just spoken it, and they can repeat it. So the open question is not knowing but doing. Verse 19 names that step: “choose life.”

passages.title: Joshua, the written law, and the song
passages.summary: Moses is 120 and tells Israel he will not cross the Jordan. The LORD and Joshua will go before them, so they must be strong. Moses writes the law and gives it to the priests and elders. Every seven years, at the feast of booths, it must be read to everyone. Men, women, children, and foreigners are to hear and learn. The LORD tells Moses the people will turn to other gods after his death. Moses writes a song to stand as a witness against them. The book of the law is placed beside the ark.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Consider how a community can preserve its commitments when a leader changes. Who must hear the law read every seven years (verses 12–13)?

contextNote.title: Public reading serves children who did not hear the first instruction
contextNote.text: Moses is about to die, and the people who heard him will die too. Verse 9 puts the law in writing and in the priests’ care. Verses 10–11 set a fixed time to read it aloud: every seventh year. Verse 12 calls men, women, little ones, and foreigners to listen. Verse 13 adds the reason: children “who have not known” must hear it. Each new generation gets the words directly, not only by report. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows the tools such writing needed.

passages.title: The Song of Moses
passages.summary: Moses sings a song and calls heaven and earth to listen. He calls God the Rock, whose work is perfect and whose ways are just. God found Israel in a desert and carried it as an eagle does. He fed Israel with honey and oil from the rock. But Israel grew fat, kicked, and left the God who made it. It turned to strange gods, so God hid his face. Yet he will judge his people and have compassion when their strength is gone. The LORD then tells Moses to climb Mount Nebo, see the land, and die there.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects the rock image with Christ. Israel “grew fat, and kicked” (verse 15). Whom did it forget?

contextNote.title: The poem turns nourishment into an image of forgotten dependence
contextNote.text: Verses 10–14 describe God feeding Israel: honey, oil, and the best of the field. Verse 15 shows what the feeding led to. The people “grew fat, and kicked,” like a well-fed animal that fights its owner. Then they left “the Rock” who saved them. Deuteronomy 8:12–14 warned of exactly this. The song gives Israel’s failure in advance, as a witness (31:19–21). Verse 36 still ends with compassion when their power is gone.

passages.title: Blessings for the tribes
passages.summary: Before he dies, Moses blesses the tribes of Israel. He says the LORD came from Sinai and loves the people. Moses gave them a law as the inheritance of all Jacob. He asks that Reuben live and that the LORD hear Judah. Levi keeps the Urim and Thummim and teaches the law. Benjamin rests in safety, and Joseph’s land is blessed with dew and deep water. Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher each get a saying. Moses ends: no one is like God, and Israel is saved by the LORD.

lds.text: How do Moses’s blessings compare with Jacob’s blessings in Genesis 49? What does verse 4 say all the tribes share?

contextNote.title: Tribal differences remain within a shared inheritance of instruction
contextNote.text: Each tribe gets its own words, and the words differ widely. Levi has holy duties, Joseph rich land, Gad a lion’s strength. Verse 4 comes before all of them and names what they share. The law Moses gave is “an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob.” Land will be divided by tribe, but this inheritance is held in common. In Genesis 49:5–7 Jacob cursed Levi’s anger. Here Levi is trusted with the Urim and Thummim (verse 8).

passages.title: Moses’s departure and Joshua’s leadership
passages.summary: Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and the LORD shows him the whole land. The LORD says this is the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses may see it but not cross over. Moses dies there in Moab, and no one knows his tomb. He was 120, with clear eyes and full strength. Israel weeps for him thirty days. Joshua is full of the spirit of wisdom, because Moses laid hands on him. No prophet like Moses has risen since, whom the LORD knew face to face.
passages.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: LDS sources teach that Moses was translated. They describe this as a change without ordinary death. What does verse 9 say prepared Joshua to lead?

contextNote.title: The end preserves both succession and the loss of Moses
contextNote.text: The book ends with a death and a handover in the same breath. Verse 8 gives the people thirty days to weep. Verse 9 says Joshua is ready, “for Moses had laid his hands on him.” The people listen to him, so the work goes on. Verse 10 does not let Joshua replace Moses in honor. No prophet since has been known by the LORD “face to face.” The loss is real, and the people still have a leader.

events.title: Moses recalls the failed entry
events.summary: Moses speaks to all Israel east of the Jordan in the fortieth year. He recalls how the LORD told them at Horeb to go and take the land. He recalls choosing leaders and judges to share his load. At Kadesh the people asked for spies, who brought back good fruit. Still the people refused to go up and said the LORD hated them. The LORD swore that generation would not see the land, except Caleb and Joshua. Moses says the LORD was angry with him too. The people then went up without the LORD and were beaten back.
events.detail: Moses is speaking to the children of the people who refused at Kadesh. He says “you” throughout, as if they had been there (verses 26–27). The parents’ choice is told as the family’s own history. In verse 37 he adds his own loss: he also will not enter. He says it was “for your sakes,” tying his fate to theirs. Numbers 20:12 gives the reason as Moses’s own act at the rock. So the speech keeps the cost of the past in front of a new generation.

lds.text: Moses tells the children what their parents did at Kadesh. What does he say about himself in verse 37?

events.title: Neighboring lands and Sihon
events.summary: Israel wandered around Mount Seir for many days. The LORD told them not to fight Esau’s people and to pay for food. He gave Moab and Ammon to Lot’s children, so Israel must leave them alone. Other peoples had also replaced earlier peoples in those lands. Thirty-eight years passed until the fighting men of the first generation died. Then the LORD gave Sihon the Amorite into Israel’s hand. Moses sent Sihon words of peace, and Sihon refused. Israel defeated him and destroyed his cities.
events.detail: Israel is on its way to land God promised. Verse 5 says the promise has edges. Mount Seir belongs to Esau, “because I have given” it to him. Verses 9 and 19 say the same of Moab and Ammon, Lot’s children. So the LORD gives land to other peoples too, and Israel must respect it. Israel is to buy food and water there, not take it (verse 6). Sihon’s land is given to Israel, and he refuses peace (verses 24–30).

lds.text: Why must Israel leave some neighboring lands alone? What reason does verse 5 give about Mount Seir?

events.title: Og, eastern settlements, and Joshua
events.summary: Og king of Bashan comes out to fight, and the LORD gives him to Israel. Israel takes his sixty walled cities. Moses gives the land east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. Their fighting men must still cross and help their brothers. Moses tells Joshua not to fear the kingdoms ahead. Moses begs the LORD to let him cross and see the good land. The LORD refuses and tells him to look from the top of Pisgah. He must strengthen Joshua, who will lead the people over.
events.detail: Moses’s prayer in verses 24–25 is personal: let me see the good land. The answer is a flat no: “Speak no more to me of this matter.” He may look from a mountain but not cross (verse 27). Verse 28 turns at once to what he can still do. He is to appoint Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him. Joshua will finish the work, and Moses must make him ready for it. Verses 21–22 show Moses already doing this.

lds.text: Moses asks to cross the Jordan, and the LORD says no (verses 25–27). What task is he given in verse 28?

events.title: Remember the covenant
events.summary: Moses tells Israel to keep the statutes and not add or take away. Other nations will call Israel wise for having such laws and so near a God. They must not forget Horeb, where the mountain burned and they heard a voice. They saw no form, so they must make no image of any creature. They must not worship the sun, moon, or stars. If they make idols, they will be scattered among the nations. Yet if they seek the LORD there with all their heart, they will find him. Moses sets apart three cities of refuge east of the Jordan.
events.detail: Verse 12 states what happened at Horeb: a voice, and no form. Verse 15 draws the rule from that fact. Because they saw no shape, they may make no shape to stand for God. Verses 16–18 close every door: human, animal, bird, creeping thing, fish. What Israel was given is words, written on two tablets (verse 13). So God is remembered by his words, taught to children (verse 9). An image would claim to show what no one saw.

lds.text: What helps you teach God’s commands with care? At Horeb Israel “saw no kind of form” (verse 15). What did they have in its place (verse 12)?

events.title: The commandments recalled
events.summary: Moses calls all Israel to hear the statutes. He says the covenant at Horeb was made with those alive today. He repeats the ten commandments. The Sabbath command says servants must rest as well as their masters. Israel must remember it was a servant in Egypt until the LORD brought it out. The LORD wrote the words on two stone tablets. The people were afraid of the fire and asked Moses to listen for them. The LORD approved and wished they would always have such a heart.
events.detail: Exodus 20:11 tied the Sabbath to God’s rest at creation. Verse 15 gives a second reason: “you were a servant in the land of Egypt.” Verse 14 says servants must rest “as well as you.” A master must remember being a slave when he sees his workers. Pharaoh gave Israel no rest (Exodus 5:5–9). So the weekly rest is a way of not becoming Pharaoh. Verse 3 adds that the covenant is with the living hearers, not only their parents.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Verse 15 gives a reason for the Sabbath. What must Israel remember?

events.title: Love, teach, and remember
events.summary: Moses gives the commandments Israel must keep in the land. The LORD is one, and Israel must love him with heart, soul, and might. These words must be on their hearts and taught to their children. They talk of them at home, on the road, at night, and at dawn. They are to tie them on hand and forehead and write them on doorposts. In the land they will have cities, houses, wells, and vineyards they did not make. Then they must not forget the LORD. When a son asks what the laws mean, the parent tells of slavery and rescue.
events.detail: Verse 5 asks for love with the whole person. Verse 6 says where the words must be: on the heart. Verse 7 turns that inward state into a daily habit with children. The four settings cover a whole day: sitting, walking, lying down, rising. No special place or teacher is named. Verses 10–12 show why the habit is needed: full houses make people forget. Verse 20 expects it to work, since the child starts asking questions.
events.uncertainty: Moab is the speech setting. Other markers show recalled places or future instructions. Regions and traditional locations are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies love for God and teaching the next generation. Verse 7 names four times to talk of God’s words. What are they?

events.title: A chosen people and severe commands
events.summary: Moses says the LORD will drive out seven nations greater than Israel. Israel is told to destroy them, make no treaty, and not marry among them. The reason given is that they would turn Israel to other gods. Israel must break their altars and burn their images. The LORD chose Israel, though it was the fewest of all peoples. He chose it because he loves it and keeps his oath to the fathers. If Israel obeys, he will bless its children, crops, and herds. The nations will be driven out little by little.
events.detail: Verses 1–5 give Israel hard orders against seven nations. Verse 6 calls Israel chosen, and verse 7 blocks a proud reading of that word. They were not more in number; they were the fewest. Verse 8 gives two reasons, and both lie in God: his love and his oath. So being chosen is not a reward for strength or goodness. events.title: Remember in prosperity
events.summary: Moses tells Israel to remember the forty years in the wilderness. God humbled them, let them hunger, and fed them with manna. He taught them that people do not live by bread alone. Their clothes did not wear out, and their feet did not swell. Now he brings them to a land of water, wheat, vines, olives, and metal. When they are full and rich, they must not forget the LORD. They must not say their own power got this wealth. If they forget and serve other gods, they will perish like the nations before them.
events.detail: The danger in this chapter is plenty, not hunger. Verses 12–13 list good houses, growing herds, silver, and gold. Verse 14 says a full heart is “lifted up” and forgets. Verse 17 gives the thought that follows: my own hand got me this wealth. In the wilderness no one could think that, since manna fell each day. Verse 18 corrects it: God gives the power to get wealth. He gives it to keep the covenant he swore, not to prove their worth.

events.title: The calf and intercession recalled
events.summary: Israel is about to cross the Jordan against nations greater and taller. The LORD will go ahead like a devouring fire. Israel must not say the land is a reward for its righteousness. The nations are driven out for their wickedness and because of God’s oath. Israel is a stubborn people, and Moses tells them to remember it. He recalls the golden calf, the broken tablets, and forty days of prayer. He names Taberah, Massah, Kibroth Hattaavah, and Kadesh. He prayed that God would remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and spare his people.

Israel gains it because of God’s oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Verse 6 adds a hard name for Israel: “a stiff-necked people.” Verses 7–24 back it up with the calf and four other failures. So possession of the land proves God’s faithfulness, not Israel’s merit.

events.title: New tablets and care for strangers
events.summary: Moses recalls cutting two new tablets and making a wooden ark for them. The LORD wrote the ten commandments again, and Moses put them in the ark. Aaron died, and the tribe of Levi was set apart to carry the ark. The LORD listened to Moses and did not destroy Israel. Now the LORD asks Israel to fear him, love him, and keep his commands. He owns heaven and earth, yet he set his love on their fathers. He takes no bribes and gives justice to the fatherless and widow. He loves the foreigner, so Israel must love the foreigner too.
events.detail: Verse 17 describes God at his greatest: God of gods, mighty, taking no bribes. Verse 18 says what that great God does. He gives justice to the fatherless and widow and feeds and clothes the foreigner. Verse 19 draws the command from his example: “Therefore love the foreigner.” It adds Israel’s own memory: “you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” So the duty has two roots, who God is and what Israel went through. events.title: Teach the words and choose a path
events.summary: Moses tells those who saw Egypt and the wilderness to love the LORD. The land ahead is not like Egypt, where they watered fields by foot. It is a land of hills and valleys that drinks rain from the sky. The LORD’s eyes are on it all year. If Israel obeys, he will send early and late rain. If they turn to other gods, he will shut the sky. They must teach these words to their children and write them on their doorposts. Moses sets a blessing and a curse before them, on Gerizim and Ebal.
events.detail: Verse 10 recalls Egyptian farming: water moved to the seed “with your foot.” The farmer there brought the water himself. Verse 11 says Canaan “drinks water from the rain of the sky.” No one can make it rain. So the new land ties each harvest to the one who sends rain (verse 14). Verses 16–17 state the risk: other gods, a shut sky, no fruit. The land itself becomes a daily lesson in dependence.

events.title: The chosen place of worship
events.summary: Israel must destroy the places where the nations served their gods. They must not worship the LORD that way, at every hill and tree. They are to bring offerings and tithes to the one place he will choose. There they eat and rejoice with sons, daughters, servants, and the Levite. They may kill and eat meat in any town, as they would a deer. But they must pour out the blood and not eat it. Holy gifts and vows still go to the chosen place. They must not copy the nations, who even burn their children for their gods.
events.detail: Verses 5–14 gather all offerings into one place that God will choose. That could seem to make every meal of meat a long journey. Verse 15 prevents this. People may kill and eat “within all your gates,” like game. The unclean and the clean may both eat it, so it is ordinary food. Only the blood rule follows them home (verse 16). The text never names the chosen place.

events.title: Tests of covenant loyalty
events.summary: A prophet may give a sign that comes true and then urge other gods. Israel must not listen, because the LORD is testing their love. That prophet is to be put to death. If a brother, child, wife, or close friend secretly urges other gods, the same applies. The one who was urged must not hide it. If a town is said to have turned, the report must be checked with care. If it is true, the town is destroyed and burned. Nothing from it may be kept.
events.detail: Verse 2 grants that the sign “comes to pass.” The test is not whether the wonder is real. The test is where the message leads: “Let’s go after other gods.” A true sign joined to that call must be refused (verse 3). So a message is judged by loyalty to the LORD who freed them (verse 5). Verse 14 adds a rule for rumor: inquire, investigate, and ask diligently. The penalties are severe, and the town’s case requires proof first.

events.title: Food, tithes, and shared provision
events.summary: Israel is the LORD’s children and must not cut themselves for the dead. They may eat cud-chewing animals with split hooves, and fish with fins and scales. Camels, hares, pigs, and many birds are forbidden. Each year they eat a tenth of their crops at the chosen place. If the way is far, they may bring money and buy food there. They must not forget the Levite. Every third year the tithe is stored in their own towns. The Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow come and eat their fill.
events.detail: In most years the family eats its tithe at the chosen place (verses 22–26). Verse 28 changes the plan every third year. The whole tithe is stored “within your gates,” in the home town. Verse 29 names four groups: the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. The Levite has no land, and the others have no secure provider. They are to “eat and be satisfied,” not just get by. The blessing on the farmer’s work is tied to this sharing.

lds.text: Every third year the tithe stays in the town (verse 28). Who eats from it in verse 29?

events.title: Release and an open hand
events.summary: Every seven years a creditor must cancel what a fellow Israelite owes. If Israel obeys, there will be no poor among them. They must open their hand to a poor brother and lend what he needs. They must not refuse a loan because the year of release is near. They must give freely, because there will always be poor in the land. A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year. He must be sent away with gifts from flock, grain, and wine. Firstborn male animals belong to the LORD.
events.detail: Verse 1 cancels debts every seventh year. That creates a temptation, and verse 9 names it. A lender could refuse a loan that will soon be wiped out. The verse calls that thought wicked, and the poor may cry to the LORD. Verse 10 asks for more than the loan: a heart that does not grudge it. Verses 13–14 say a freed servant must not leave empty-handed. Verse 15 gives the reason: Israel was a slave, and the LORD redeemed it.

events.title: Festivals and fair judgment
events.summary: Israel keeps the Passover in the month of Abib, at the place the LORD chooses. They eat unleavened bread seven days, the bread of affliction. Seven weeks after harvest begins, they keep the feast of weeks with a free gift. They rejoice with children, servants, Levites, foreigners, the fatherless, and widows. They keep the feast of booths seven days after the harvest is in. Three times a year the men come before the LORD with a gift. Judges in every town must judge fairly and take no bribe. No sacred pole or pillar may stand by the LORD’s altar.
events.detail: The feast of weeks comes at harvest, when a landowner has the most. Verse 11 says who must rejoice with him. The list starts with his children and servants. It goes on to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. Verse 14 repeats the same list for the feast of booths. Verse 12 gives the reason: “you were a slave in Egypt.” A feast kept only by the harvest’s owners is not the feast commanded here.

events.title: Judges and limits on kings
events.summary: No animal with a defect may be offered to the LORD. Serving other gods brings death, but only on two or three witnesses. Hard cases go to the priests and the judge at the chosen place. Their verdict must be followed. Israel may one day ask for a king like other nations. He must be an Israelite whom the LORD chooses. He must not collect many horses, wives, or much silver and gold. He must write his own copy of this law and read it all his life.
events.detail: Verses 16–17 limit three things a king might gather: horses, wives, and treasure. Verse 16 ties horses to going back to Egypt, which is forbidden. Verses 18–19 give him a task: copy the law and read it daily. Verse 20 states the aim: “that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers.” The king is called a brother and stays under the same law as everyone. First Kings 10:26–11:4 reports that Solomon broke all three limits.

lds.text: Which rules stop a king from using his power only for himself (verses 16–17)? What must he read every day (verses 18–19)?

events.title: Priests and a prophet like Moses
events.summary: The priests and Levites have no land, and the LORD is their inheritance. They receive set parts of sacrifices and the first of grain, wine, oil, and wool. A Levite from any town may come and serve at the chosen place. Israel must not copy the nations who burn children, tell fortunes, or consult the dead. The LORD will raise up a prophet like Moses from among them. Israel asked for this at Horeb, when they feared God’s voice. A prophet who speaks falsely in God’s name must die. If what a prophet says does not happen, the LORD did not say it.
events.detail: Verses 10–14 forbid the usual ways of learning the future: fortunes, omens, the dead. Verse 15 gives Israel a prophet in their place. That raises a problem, and verse 21 asks it openly. How can people tell a true word from a false one? Verse 22 gives a test anyone can apply: watch whether it happens. A failed word frees the people from fear of that speaker. Chapter 13 added a second test: a sign that comes true may still lead astray.

events.title: Refuge, boundaries, and witnesses
events.summary: Israel must set apart three cities in the land for anyone who kills by accident. An example is an ax head that flies off and strikes a neighbor. The cities keep the avenger from killing him in hot anger. If the land grows, three more cities are added. A man who kills from hatred is handed over to die. No one may move a neighbor’s boundary stone. A charge needs two or three witnesses, not one. A false witness receives the penalty he meant for the other person.
events.detail: A single accuser can be mistaken or can lie. Verse 15 says no charge of any kind stands on one voice. Two or three must agree. Verses 16–18 deal with a witness who lies on purpose. The judges must “make diligent inquisition” and not simply take his word. If he lied, he gets the penalty he sought for his brother (verse 19). So the court protects the accused as well as the victim.

events.title: Rules for warfare
events.summary: Before battle a priest tells the army the LORD fights for them. Officers send home men with a new house, vineyard, or bride. They also send home anyone who is afraid. A distant city must first be offered peace. If it refuses, its men are killed and the rest are taken. Cities of the land itself must be destroyed, to keep Israel from their gods. During a long siege Israel must not cut down fruit trees. Only trees that give no food may be used for siege works.
events.detail: This chapter holds limits and harsh orders side by side. Verses 5–8 send men home for a house, a vineyard, a marriage, or fear. Verse 10 requires an offer of peace before a siege. Verses 16–17 order the complete destruction of the cities of the land. Verse 19 then protects fruit trees with a question: is the tree a man? An army will need that food later, and the tree has not fought anyone. The text restrains waste while it commands killing, and it does not reconcile the two.

events.title: Unsolved killing and household laws
events.summary: When a slain body is found and no killer is known, the nearest elders act. They break a heifer’s neck, wash their hands, and ask the LORD’s forgiveness. A soldier who marries a captive woman must first give her a month to mourn. If he later sends her away, he may not sell her. A man with two wives must give the firstborn’s double share to the true firstborn. He may not favor the son of the wife he loves. Parents may bring a stubborn, rebellious son to the elders, and he is stoned. A hanged body must be buried the same day.
events.detail: Verse 15 pictures a man with two wives, one loved and one “hated.” Jacob’s house was like that, with Leah and Rachel (Genesis 29:30–31). The father might want to honor the loved wife’s son. Verse 16 says he may not. Verse 17 gives the double share to the actual firstborn, whoever his mother is. So a son’s right does not depend on his father’s feelings toward his mother. The law limits a father’s power inside his own house.

events.title: Neighborly care and sexual laws
events.summary: Anyone who finds a neighbor’s stray animal or lost item must return it. A fallen animal must be helped up. A mother bird must be let go when the young are taken. A new house needs a railing around its roof so no one falls. Seeds, plow animals, and cloth types must not be mixed. A husband who falsely accuses his bride is fined, and a guilty bride is stoned. Adultery brings death for both. A woman forced in the open country is not guilty, and only the man dies.

If he does not and someone falls, the blood is “on your house.” So a person answers for a danger he could foresee and did not fix. Verses 1–4 say the same about a neighbor’s animals: “You may not hide yourself.” Doing nothing is treated as a choice.

events.title: Assembly, camp, and promises
events.summary: Some people may not enter the LORD’s assembly. Ammonites and Moabites are barred, because they refused bread and hired Balaam. Edomites and Egyptians are not to be hated, and their third generation may enter. The army camp must be kept clean, because the LORD walks in it. An escaped servant must not be handed back to his master. He may live where he chooses and must not be oppressed. Israel must not charge a brother interest and must pay its vows. A person may eat in a neighbor’s field but not carry food away.

He may settle “where it pleases him best,” and no one may oppress him. Israel had itself fled from a master (Exodus 14:5). Verse 7 uses the same memory to forbid hating Egyptians. The rule places the escaped person’s safety above the owner’s claim.

events.title: Household changes and protection of the poor
events.summary: A man who divorces his wife gives her a written certificate. If she remarries and is free again, the first husband may not take her back. A newly married man stays home from war for a year. No one may take a millstone as a pledge, because it is a person’s living. A lender waits outside for a pledge and returns a poor man’s cloak by sunset. A hired worker must be paid the same day. Each person dies for his own sin, not a parent’s or child’s. Forgotten sheaves, olives, and grapes are left for foreigners, the fatherless, and widows.

The verse covers foreigners as well as Israelites (verse 14). It warns that the worker may cry to the LORD against the employer. Verses 6 and 10–13 protect the same people from lenders. Verse 18 gives the ground for all of it: “you were a slave in Egypt.”

events.title: Fair measures and family continuity
events.summary: Judges must clear the innocent and condemn the guilty. A beating may not go past forty strokes, so the person is not degraded. An ox must not be muzzled while it treads grain. If a man dies without a son, his brother should marry the widow. If the brother refuses, she removes his sandal before the elders. Israel must not keep two sets of weights or measures. Weights and measures must be full and fair. Israel must remember how Amalek attacked the weak at the rear.

Verse 15 requires one “perfect and just” weight and measure. The reward promised is long life in the land, as for honoring parents (5:16). Verse 16 calls dishonest dealing an abomination to the LORD. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the rule has in view.

events.title: First produce and covenant declaration
events.summary: In the land, each Israelite brings a basket of first fruits to the priest. He says that he has come to the land the LORD swore to give. He says his father was a Syrian near death who went to Egypt. Egypt made them slaves, and the LORD heard their cry and brought them out. Now he brings the first of what the LORD gave. He rejoices with the Levite and the foreigner. In the third year he gives the tithe to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow. Israel declares the LORD is its God, and the LORD declares Israel his own people.

His words in verse 5 start somewhere else: “a Syrian ready to perish.” He names an ancestor with no land and few people. Verses 6–8 go through slavery, a cry, and rescue. Only in verse 10 does he reach the basket. So the gift is set inside a history of weakness and help. Verse 11 then shares the joy with the Levite and the foreigner.

events.title: Instructions for Ebal and Gerizim
events.summary: After crossing the Jordan, the people must set up large plastered stones. They must write the law on them plainly, on Mount Ebal. They build an altar there of uncut stones. Six tribes stand on Gerizim to bless and six on Ebal for the curse. The Levites call out twelve curses in a loud voice. The curses name secret idols, dishonoring parents, and moving a boundary stone. They name misleading the blind, denying justice to the weak, and secret killing. After each one, all the people answer, “Amen.”

A moved boundary stone or a bribe may never reach a court. Verse 18 names the blind traveler, who cannot see who misled him. So the list covers wrongs that witnesses and judges would miss. events.title: Blessings and terrible curses
events.summary: If Israel listens to the LORD, blessings will overtake them. They will be blessed in city and field, in children, crops, and herds. The LORD will send rain, and they will lend and not borrow. If they do not listen, curses will overtake them. They will suffer sickness, drought, defeat, and loss of all they work for. A far nation whose language they do not know will besiege their towns. They will be scattered among the nations and find no rest. They will even be offered as slaves in Egypt, and no one will buy them.

Israel did not serve the LORD “with joyfulness” when it had “abundance of all things.” Verse 48 turns each good into its loss: hunger, thirst, nakedness, and lack. The chapter ends in Egypt, where the story of rescue began (verse 68). It warns a nation before it enters the land. It is not a rule for judging one sufferer.

events.title: The covenant assembly
events.summary: Moses gathers all Israel in Moab for a covenant beyond the one at Horeb. He recalls Egypt and forty years when their clothes did not wear out. Everyone stands before the LORD: leaders, men, children, wives, and foreigners. Even the woodcutter and the water carrier are there. The covenant is also made with those not present that day. No one who turns to other gods in secret will be pardoned. Later nations will ask why the land was ruined and hear the reason. Secret things belong to the LORD, and revealed things to Israel and its children.
events.detail: Verse 10 begins the list with heads, elders, and officers. Verse 11 goes on to little ones, wives, and foreigners in the camp. It ends with the lowest jobs: cutting wood and drawing water. All of them “stand today” before the LORD and enter the covenant. Verses 14–15 stretch it further, to people not yet born. So the covenant is not held only by leaders or fighting men. Verse 29 gives everyone the same task: do the words that have been revealed.

events.title: Return and choose life
events.summary: When scattered Israel returns to the LORD, he will gather them. He will bring them back from the farthest places. He will change their hearts so they love him and live. The command is not too hard or too far away. It is not in heaven or across the sea. The word is very near, in their mouth and heart. Moses sets life and death, blessing and curse, before them. He tells them to choose life by loving the LORD and holding to him.
events.detail: Verses 12–13 answer two excuses before anyone makes them. The command is not up in heaven, and it is not across the sea. No one has to fetch it. Verse 14 says where it already is: “in your mouth and in your heart.” Moses has just spoken it, and they can repeat it. So the open question is not knowing but doing. Verse 19 names that step: “choose life.”

events.title: Joshua, the written law, and the song
events.summary: Moses is 120 and tells Israel he will not cross the Jordan. The LORD and Joshua will go before them, so they must be strong. Moses writes the law and gives it to the priests and elders. Every seven years, at the feast of booths, it must be read to everyone. Men, women, children, and foreigners are to hear and learn. The LORD tells Moses the people will turn to other gods after his death. Moses writes a song to stand as a witness against them. The book of the law is placed beside the ark.
events.detail: Moses is about to die, and the people who heard him will die too. Verse 9 puts the law in writing and in the priests’ care. Verses 10–11 set a fixed time to read it aloud: every seventh year. Verse 12 calls men, women, little ones, and foreigners to listen. Verse 13 adds the reason: children “who have not known” must hear it. Each new generation gets the words directly, not only by report. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows the tools such writing needed.

events.title: The Song of Moses
events.summary: Moses sings a song and calls heaven and earth to listen. He calls God the Rock, whose work is perfect and whose ways are just. God found Israel in a desert and carried it as an eagle does. He fed Israel with honey and oil from the rock. But Israel grew fat, kicked, and left the God who made it. It turned to strange gods, so God hid his face. Yet he will judge his people and have compassion when their strength is gone. The LORD then tells Moses to climb Mount Nebo, see the land, and die there.
events.detail: Verses 10–14 describe God feeding Israel: honey, oil, and the best of the field. Verse 15 shows what the feeding led to. The people “grew fat, and kicked,” like a well-fed animal that fights its owner. Then they left “the Rock” who saved them. Deuteronomy 8:12–14 warned of exactly this. events.title: Blessings for the tribes
events.summary: Before he dies, Moses blesses the tribes of Israel. He says the LORD came from Sinai and loves the people. Moses gave them a law as the inheritance of all Jacob. He asks that Reuben live and that the LORD hear Judah. Levi keeps the Urim and Thummim and teaches the law. Benjamin rests in safety, and Joseph’s land is blessed with dew and deep water. Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher each get a saying. Moses ends: no one is like God, and Israel is saved by the LORD.
events.detail: Each tribe gets its own words, and the words differ widely. Levi has holy duties, Joseph rich land, Gad a lion’s strength. Verse 4 comes before all of them and names what they share. The law Moses gave is “an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob.” Land will be divided by tribe, but this inheritance is held in common. In Genesis 49:5–7 Jacob cursed Levi’s anger. Here Levi is trusted with the Urim and Thummim (verse 8).

events.title: Moses’s departure and Joshua’s leadership
events.summary: Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and the LORD shows him the whole land. The LORD says this is the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses may see it but not cross over. Moses dies there in Moab, and no one knows his tomb. He was 120, with clear eyes and full strength. Israel weeps for him thirty days. Joshua is full of the spirit of wisdom, because Moses laid hands on him. No prophet like Moses has risen since, whom the LORD knew face to face.
events.detail: The book ends with a death and a handover in the same breath. Verse 8 gives the people thirty days to weep. Verse 9 says Joshua is ready, “for Moses had laid his hands on him.” The people listen to him, so the work goes on. Verse 10 does not let Joshua replace Moses in honor. No prophet since has been known by the LORD “face to face.” The loss is real, and the people still have a leader.

words.label: Circumcision
words.meaning: The cutting of the foreskin. Genesis 17 makes it the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham.

words.label: Atonement

words.label: Tithe

guides.title: Deuteronomy: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Memory needs daily practice
steps.text: Verse 5 asks for love with the whole person. Verse 6 says where the words must be: on the heart. Verse 7 turns that inward state into a daily habit with children. The four settings cover a whole day: sitting, walking, lying down, rising. No special place or teacher is named. Verses 10–12 show why the habit is needed: full houses make people forget. Verse 20 expects it to work, since the child starts asking questions.

steps.title: The king must live under the law
steps.text: Verses 16–17 limit three things a king might gather: horses, wives, and treasure. Verse 16 ties horses to going back to Egypt, which is forbidden. Verses 18–19 give him a task: copy the law and read it daily. Verse 20 states the aim: “that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers.” The king is called a brother and stays under the same law as everyone. First Kings 10:26–11:4 reports that Solomon broke all three limits.

steps.title: Small measures can cause real harm
steps.text: Goods were weighed against weights kept in a bag. Verse 13 pictures a cheat with two sets, one heavy and one light. The buyer has no way to test them. Verse 15 requires one “perfect and just” weight and measure. The reward promised is long life in the land, as for honoring parents (5:16). Verse 16 calls dishonest dealing an abomination to the LORD. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the rule has in view.

He says his father was a Syrian near death who went to Egypt. Egypt made them slaves, and the LORD heard their cry and brought them out. Now he brings the first of what the LORD gave. He rejoices with the Levite and the foreigner. In the third year he gives the tithe to the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow. Israel declares the LORD is its God, and the LORD declares Israel his own people.

chapterMaps.narrative: After crossing the Jordan, the people must set up large plastered stones. They must write the law on them plainly, on Mount Ebal. They build an altar there of uncut stones. Six tribes stand on Gerizim to bless and six on Ebal for the curse. The Levites call out twelve curses in a loud voice. The curses name secret idols, dishonoring parents, and moving a boundary stone. They name misleading the blind, denying justice to the weak, and secret killing. After each one, all the people answer, “Amen.”

chapterMaps.narrative: If Israel listens to the LORD, blessings will overtake them. They will be blessed in city and field, in children, crops, and herds. The LORD will send rain, and they will lend and not borrow. If they do not listen, curses will overtake them. They will suffer sickness, drought, defeat, and loss of all they work for. A far nation whose language they do not know will besiege their towns. They will be scattered among the nations and find no rest. They will even be offered as slaves in Egypt, and no one will buy them.
